w: Laid down in 1943 at Electric Boat's yard in Groton, Connecticut, this Gato-class submarine is best known for sinking the Japanese aircraft carrier Shokaku. Commissioned in February 1944 under Lt. Cmdr. Herman Kossler, she is now preserved as a museum ship.
s: Submarine that sank a Japanese carrier
_facts: Gato-class submarine, keel laid 1943 by Electric Boat Co, Groton CT
Best known for sinking Japanese aircraft carrier Shokaku
Commissioned 29 Feb 1944 under Lt Cmdr Herman J Kossler
Preserved today as a museum ship

w: Opened in 1911 as Hotel Galvez, named for Bernardo de Galvez, the Spanish viscount for whom the city itself is named, this 226-room resort was Galveston's answer to rebuilding after the 1900 hurricane. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, it is a member of Historic Hotels of America.
s: 1911 resort named for the city's own namesake
_facts: Opened 1911 as Hotel Galvez, 226 rooms
Named for Bernardo de Galvez, 1st Viscount of Galveston
Added to National Register of Historic Places, 4 April 1979
Member of Historic Hotels of America

w: Commissioned in 1968, this Sturgeon-class attack submarine was the second US Navy vessel named for the tautog, a wrasse common along the Northern Atlantic coast. She served through the Cold War until decommissioning in 1997, and is now preserved as a museum ship.
s: Cold War attack sub named after an Atlantic fish
_facts: Sturgeon-class nuclear-powered attack submarine
In commission 17 August 1968 to 31 March 1997
Named for the tautog, an Atlantic wrasse
Preserved today as a museum ship

w: The current building went up in 1848, replacing Galveston's original 1842 wooden church, and became the mother church of Texas Catholics once dedicated. It escaped serious damage in the 1900 hurricane, was named a minor basilica in 2004, then flooded during Hurricane Ike in 2008 -- reopening in 2014 after repairs.
s: Mother church of Texas Catholics, survivor of two hurricanes
_facts: Built 1848, replacing an 1842 wooden church
Mother church of over 1.5 million Catholics in the archdiocese
Escaped major damage in the 1900 hurricane; flooded by Hurricane Ike, 2008
Elevated to minor basilica in 2004; reopened 2014 after repairs

w: Launched in 1877, this three-masted iron barque is among the oldest ships still sailing anywhere. Rescued and restored at the Galveston Historic Seaport, she was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1990, and the Texas Legislature named her the state's official tall ship in 2005.
s: 1877 tall ship, still sailing, Texas's official vessel
_facts: Three-masted barque launched in 1877
One of the oldest ships still sailing today
National Historic Landmark since 1990
Named Texas's official tall ship in 2005

w: Named for Charles Stewart, who commanded USS Constitution in the War of 1812, this Edsall-class destroyer escort is one of only two of her type preserved in the US -- and the only Edsall-class ship left at all. She is moored at Seawolf Park on Pelican Island, open to the public as a museum ship.
s: The last surviving Edsall-class destroyer escort
_facts: Edsall-class destroyer escort, named for Rear Adm. Charles Stewart
One of only two preserved US destroyer escorts, the only Edsall-class survivor
Displayed as a museum ship at Seawolf Park, Pelican Island

w: Built on a pier stretching 600 feet over the Gulf, this nightclub and illegal casino was run by Sicilian bootleggers-turned-barbers Sam and Rosario Maceo through Galveston's 1930s-40s 'open era.' Sinatra, Bob Hope and the Marx Brothers played it; Howard Hughes was a regular. Ike tore it into the sea in 2008.
s: Mob-run casino pier that hosted Sinatra and Hughes
_facts: Nightclub and illegal casino on a 600-ft pier over the Gulf of Mexico
Run by Sam and Rosario Maceo during Galveston's 1930s-40s 'open era'
Entertainers included Sinatra, Bob Hope, the Marx Brothers; patrons included Howard Hughes
Listed on NRHP 1997; destroyed by Hurricane Ike, 13 September 2008

w: Built to defend Galveston's harbor and the oil ports beyond it, this coastal artillery reservation once guarded the entrance to Galveston Bay from the Gulf. It has since passed to NOAA's fisheries service and the Texas Institute of Oceanography, but several original fortifications and historic buildings still stand.
s: Coastal gun battery guarding Galveston's harbor mouth
_facts: Government reservation built as a coastal defense installation
Protected Galveston Bay's entrance and the region's oil ports
Now managed by NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Service
Retains several historic buildings and military fortifications

w: Known simply as 'Old Red' for its red brick and sandstone, this 1891 Romanesque Revival building by Nicholas Clayton was the first home of the University of Texas Medical Branch. It survived the devastating 1900 hurricane virtually intact, only to be swamped by six feet of floodwater during Hurricane Ike in 2008.
s: Old Red: an 1891 building that outlasted two hurricanes
_facts: Built 1891 in red brick and sandstone by architect Nicholas J. Clayton
First building of the University of Texas Medical Branch
Survived the 1900 Galveston hurricane largely intact
Flooded with six feet of water during Hurricane Ike, 2008

w: Unveiled on July 25, 2014 in R.A. Apffel Park on East Beach, this public sculpture was the first monument in the entire southern United States dedicated to gender and sexual minority communities. It stands as a quiet, easy-to-miss civic landmark on Galveston's eastern shoreline.
s: The South's first monument to LGBT communities
_facts: Public sculpture in R.A. Apffel Park / East Beach
Inaugurated 25 July 2014
First monument dedicated to gender and sexual minorities in the southern US
